title: Exploring the 6th-Century Christian Topography

pages.text: The Christian Topography is a very old book written in the sixth century. It is one of the earliest geographical essays by a Christian author. A writer named Cosmas wrote the book. He was also known as Indicopleustes because he sailed to India long ago.
pages.caption: Ancient world map, from Christian Topography, by Cosmas Indicopleustes.

evidence.articleCaption: Ancient world map, from Christian Topography, by Cosmas Indicopleustes.

pages.text: The book originally had five books. Later, the author added more books until there were twelve books in total. The text talked about different parts of the world. It also included maps and illustrations to help explain the ideas of the writer.

Cosmas put forward the idea that the world is flat. He wrote that the heavens form the shape of a box with a curved lid. Most other Christians of that time believed the Earth was a sphere instead of flat.

The author used passages from scriptures to support his thesis. He argued against the idea of a spherical Earth and called it pagan. Some monks also criticized his views, and Cosmas wrote to rebut their criticism.

The place of Cosmas in history has sometimes been misunderstood. His work was not the main authority of the Middle Ages in geography, as its influence was only slightly and occasionally traceable. Yet the Christian Topography remains remarkable as one of the earliest important essays in scientific geography within the Christian era written by a Christian thinker.

Today, only a few nearly complete manuscripts of this ancient work survive. The earliest and best manuscript is from the ninth century in the Vatican Library. Other copies from the eleventh century are kept in monasteries.

The Christian Topography is a sixth-century work and one of the earliest essays in scientific geography written by a Christian author. Originally consisting of five books by Cosmas Indicopleustes, the text was later expanded to twelve books around 550 AD.

pages.text: The author, Cosmas Indicopleustes, proposed the controversial idea that the world is flat and that the heavens resemble a box with a curved lid. Although most Christians and scholars of that period maintained that the Earth was a sphere, Cosmas rejected the geocentric model.

To support his claims, Cosmas cited scriptural passages and dismissed the spherical Earth theory as pagan. His ideas faced opposition from fellow monks and contemporaries, such as John Philoponus, who wrote a direct refutation of his work.

Despite his unusual cosmology, Cosmas was an experienced traveller who visited the Red Sea coast and modern Sri Lanka. His book offers valuable insights into Byzantine geographical knowledge and includes descriptions of places like Axum and trade routes.

The work's historical influence was generally marginal, and it was never the chief geographical authority of the Middle Ages. However, scholars note that it is frequently miscited today as proof that medieval people universally believed in a flat Earth.

Only three nearly complete manuscripts of the text survive today. The earliest, housed in the Vatican Library, dates from the ninth century and contains ten books, while two eleventh-century manuscripts contain the full twelve books.

Authored in the sixth century, the Christian Topography stands as a pioneering essay in scientific geography by a Christian writer. Initiated as a five-book treatise by Cosmas Indicopleustes, the text underwent successive expansions until reaching twelve books around 550 AD.

pages.text: Central to the work is the idiosyncratic cosmological thesis that the Earth is flat and enclosed by a box-shaped heaven with a curved lid. This assertion directly opposed the prevailing scholarly consensus of the era, which overwhelmingly favored a spherical Earth model.

Cosmas attempted to substantiate his arguments through novel interpretations of scripture while stigmatizing spherical geography as pagan. This provoked domestic criticism from fellow monastics, as well as formal scholarly rebuttals from contemporaries like John Philoponus.

Beyond its cosmological digressions, the treatise preserves substantive geographical data derived from the author's personal travels along the Red Sea and to Sri Lanka. These eyewitness observations provide rare contemporary documentation of sixth-century trade networks and political events.

Although historical reception was decidedly marginal and failed to dominate medieval geographical thought, the text occupies an important historiographical role. Modern scholars frequently cite it to correct misconceptions regarding the prevalence of flat-Earth beliefs in medieval Europe.

Textual transmission relies upon three surviving nearly complete manuscript witnesses. The ninth-century Vatican manuscript preserves ten books, whereas two eleventh-century exemplars from Saint Catherine's Monastery and Mount Athos contain the complete twelve-book recension.

title: History and Growth of the Summer Olympics

A1-A2.headline: The Story of the Summer Olympics

pages.text: The Summer Olympic Games are a big global sports event. They happen normally every four years. The very first modern Games took place in Athens, Greece, in 1896. Pierre de Coubertin started the group that runs them, called the International Olympic Committee.
pages.caption: The 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, Australia, were known as the "Games of the New Millennium".

evidence.fileTitle: File:2000 Sydney Women's long jump final.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, Australia, were known as the "Games of the New Millennium".

pages.text: In 1896, only 14 countries came to the Games. There were fewer than 250 competitors, and all of them were men. Women could not take part in those first events. Women first took part officially in the Paris Games in the year 1900.

Over time, the Games grew much bigger. By the 2021 Games in Tokyo, thousands of competitors came from 206 nations. Almost half of these athletes were women. Countries all over the world have hosted this huge international multi-sport event.
pages.caption: Map of Summer Olympic Games locations – countries that have hosted one Summer Olympics are shaded green, while countries that have hosted two or more are shaded blue.

evidence.articleCaption: Map of Summer Olympic Games locations – countries that have hosted one Summer Olympics are shaded green, while countries that have hosted two or more are shaded blue.

pages.text: Cities in many different countries want to host the Olympics. London and Paris have hosted the Games three times. Other places like Los Angeles, Athens, and Tokyo have hosted them twice. Hosting brings big changes and new investments to city infrastructure.

Australia, France, and Great Britain are the only countries that have won at least one medal in every single Summer Games. Great Britain is the only country to win at least one gold medal in every single edition of the event.

The United States has hosted the Summer Olympics four times in cities like St. Louis, Los Angeles, and Atlanta. The U.S. also leads the all-time medal count. The Games continue to change today, adding new sports for athletes to play.

B1-B2.headline: History and Growth of the Summer Olympics

pages.text: The Summer Olympic Games are the world's largest and most prestigious multi-sport international event. Usually held once every four years, the modern tradition began in Athens. The International Olympic Committee, founded by Pierre de Coubertin, organized this groundbreaking global competition.
pages.caption: The 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, Australia, were known as the "Games of the New Millennium".

evidence.fileTitle: File:2000 Sydney Women's long jump final.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, Australia, were known as the "Games of the New Millennium".

pages.text: The inaugural 1896 Games featured just 42 events with fewer than 250 male competitors from 14 nations. Female athletes were initially excluded, though women officially joined the competition at the 1900 Paris Games. Participation expanded dramatically over the decades, reaching 11,319 competitors from 206 nations by 2021.

Cities worldwide have competed to host the Olympics, spreading the event across five continents. London and Paris have hosted three times, while Los Angeles, Athens, and Tokyo have hosted twice. Rio de Janeiro hosted the first South American Games in 2016 amid various local challenges.
pages.caption: Map of Summer Olympic Games locations – countries that have hosted one Summer Olympics are shaded green, while countries that have hosted two or more are shaded blue.

evidence.articleCaption: Map of Summer Olympic Games locations – countries that have hosted one Summer Olympics are shaded green, while countries that have hosted two or more are shaded blue.

pages.text: Only three countries have won at least one medal in every Summer Games: Australia, France, and Great Britain. Furthermore, Great Britain stands alone as the only nation to secure at least one gold medal in every single edition. The United States leads the all-time medal count.

Hosting the Olympics requires massive investments in local infrastructure, playing a key role in urban development and global integration. Preparing for these massive gatherings often involves significant political, economic, and logistical efforts from the host cities and nations.

The sports programme has evolved continually since the early Games. The 2024 Games featured 32 sports, while future editions plan to introduce entirely new disciplines like flag football and squash. International sports federations govern the qualification rules for each specific competition.

C1-C2.headline: Evolution of the Modern Summer Olympics

pages.text: Evolving from nineteenth-century ideals of international understanding, the Summer Olympic Games were established by Pierre de Coubertin through the founding of the International Olympic Committee in 1894. The inaugural 1896 Games in Athens inaugurated a quadrennial tradition that subsequently became the world's preeminent international multi-sport gathering.
pages.caption: The 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, Australia, were known as the "Games of the New Millennium".

evidence.fileTitle: File:2000 Sydney Women's long jump final.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, Australia, were known as the "Games of the New Millennium".

pages.text: The scope of the competition expanded exponentially from the 1896 programme of 42 events and under 250 male athletes to thousands of competitors across 206 nations by 2021. Although female participation was absent initially, women debuted officially in 1900, eventually comprising nearly half of all athletes in contemporary editions.

Geographically, the Games have spanned nineteen countries across five continents. Cities such as London and Paris achieved multiple hosting duties, while Rio de Janeiro marked South America's inaugural hosting milestone in 2016 amidst complex socioeconomic and health controversies.

evidence.articleCaption: Map of Summer Olympic Games locations – countries that have hosted one Summer Olympics are shaded green, while countries that have hosted two or more are shaded blue.

pages.text: Competitive dominance remains concentrated among specific nations. Australia, France, and Great Britain share the distinction of securing medals in every Summer Games, with Great Britain uniquely capturing at least one gold medal in every edition. The United States leads the cumulative medal standings comprehensively.

Infrastructure enhancement remains inextricably linked to hosting responsibilities, as municipal leaders leverage the Games to accelerate urban development and enhance global economic competitiveness. Such capital investments demand substantial financial commitments, exemplified by security and operational expenditures in modern editions.

The athletic programme has adapted continuously, transitioning from historical roots to include 32 sports in recent programmes and planned expansions into emerging disciplines. Governing International Sports Federations autonomously regulate qualification protocols, while the IOC categorizes sports based on global popularity metrics.
